title: On Consensus and Humming in the IETF
summary: Explains how the IETF's rough consensus process is meant to work and why it is not majority voting. It argues the IETF has drifted toward vote-like behavior and suggests ways to get back to real rough consensus. It is informational and does not change process.

plainLanguage.summary: The IETF decides by consensus rather than by voting, which means every objection has to be dealt with rather than outvoted. This RFC explains what that means in practice, why a hum in a meeting is only a way to start the discussion, and why counting voices cannot settle a question.

questions: how does the ietf make decisions
subtitle: Why the IETF decides by open issues rather than by votes, and what humming is really for.

tldr.problem: Participants and chairs often treat a hum or a poll as a vote, then ask why the discussion is not over once a hum has happened. Working groups end up factious, with long-running unresolved issues and bad compromises.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC explains that rough consensus means every objection has been addressed, though not necessarily accommodated. Counting heads does not decide it, and a hum is only a way to start the conversation. It then shows that a hundred voices for a protocol cannot rescue an unaddressed objection, and that five informed voices can outweigh a hundred who bring no new information.
tldr.outcome: It is an Informational RFC that calls for thought and discussion rather than a new procedure. It prescribes nothing, and says that many current practices are not consistent with the principles it describes.

today: RFC 7282 is an Informational RFC published in June 2014. It has not been obsoleted or updated. It describes principles rather than a fixed procedure, and it says it is meant to generate thought and discussion.

sections.title: The Credo and the Misreadings
sections.content:
Almost every participant knows the aphorism from Dave Clark's 1992 plenary presentation about how decisions are made in the IETF: we reject kings, presidents and voting; we believe in rough consensus and running code. The credo is that no single individual dictates decisions, nor should decisions be made by a vote, nor should they be made in a vacuum without practical experience. Instead the community strives to make decisions by the consent of all participants, allowing some dissent, and to have the products of engineering trump theoretical designs.

Full consensus, or unanimity, would be ideal but is not required, because requiring it lets a single intransigent person who keeps saying no stop the process cold. What is required is rough consensus. If the chair of a working group determines that a technical issue brought forward by an objector has been truly considered, and that the working group has made an informed decision that the objection has been answered or is not enough of a technical problem to prevent moving forward, the chair can declare that there is rough consensus, the objection notwithstanding.

To reinforce that the IETF does not vote, the community adopted the tradition of humming: at a face-to-face meeting, instead of a show of hands, a chair sometimes asks each side to hum on a question, either for or against. The RFC says that in recent years participants, and even some in IETF leadership, have not understood some of the subtleties. They ask why they cannot just vote, or why the discussion is not concluded once they have hummed or voted. Chairs, many of whom have little experience in leading large volunteer groups, are left with factious working groups, polarized viewpoints, long-running unresolved issues that return to the agenda again and again, and participants walking away feeling that consensus produced a document full of bad compromises to satisfy everyone's pet peeve instead of doing the right thing. None of that indicates a rough consensus process being used, and the RFC attributes it to basic misperceptions.

The document explains what rough consensus is, what it is not, some new ways to think about it, and where the IETF might achieve and judge it. It talks about the behaviour of working groups and chairs in broad brushstrokes and does not prescribe specific procedures. Its purpose is to foster understanding of the underlying principles, and it is aimed at people with experience in the IETF, especially those who might lead a consensus discussion.
sections.plainLanguage: The IETF has no boss and does not count votes. A chair can move on once the objections have been dealt with, even if one person still disagrees. The RFC says that treating a hum as a vote is what is breaking things.

sections.title: Agreement Is Not the Goal
sections.content:
A working group faces a question of whether to use format A or format B. The chair asks on the mailing list whether everyone is happy with format A, and inevitably a number of people object for various technical reasons. The chair then asks about format B, and even more people object on different technical grounds. The chair, having agreement on neither, is left thinking the group has deadlocked.

The problem is that the chair was looking for agreement. Determining consensus, coming to consensus and having consensus are three different things. Engineering always involves trade-offs, so any choice will have options that appeal to some people and not to others. In determining consensus the key is to separate choices that are simply unappealing from those that are truly problematic. If some people did not get their preferred choice but have become convinced that the chosen solution is acceptable, albeit less appealing, the group has still come to consensus. Consensus does not require that everyone is happy, but it does require that everyone is sufficiently satisfied that they no longer have specific objections.

So it matters most to ask not just for objections but for the nature of them. A chair who asks whether everyone is happy with choice A will get objections; a chair who asks who cannot live with choice A is more likely to hear only from those who think it cannot be engineered at all. Following up with the reasons is essential, so that the purported failings can be examined. The objector might convince the group, or the group might convince the objector that the concerns can be addressed or that the choice is merely unappealing. Closure comes faster from asking for and accommodating objections than from asking for agreement.

Sorting out disagreement is not the only thing needed. A solution with no objections but no support either is not consensus: the group needs the active engagement and eventual support of the people doing the work. But mere agreement among participants is not enough either. People might agree that a solution is sufficient and have no objection to it, yet not actively think it is a good and correct outcome, and declaring consensus on that basis is absurd.

The word compromise is used in two different ways, and the RFC separates them. Compromising between engineering principles is expected and essential: giving up processor speed for lower power consumption, or throughput for congestion resistance, and collectively choosing the set that best meets the full set of requirements. Compromising between people is another matter. A minority that still thinks a proposal is deeply problematic may decide they lack the energy to argue and say, forget it, do what you want. A chair might take that for agreement and declare consensus, but what has happened is capitulation: there is still an outstanding unaddressed objection. Worse is horse-trading, where each side stops objecting if the other does, which leaves two objections open rather than one. Neither capitulation nor horse-trading has any place in consensus decision making, and answering technical disagreements is what is needed, sometimes even when the people who raised them no longer wish to discuss them.
sections.plainLanguage: Asking who agrees gets you arguments. Asking who cannot live with a choice finds the real problems. Giving up a real objection because you are tired is not agreement, and trading objections away leaves two problems instead of one.

sections.title: Addressed, but Not Necessarily Accommodated
sections.content:
Often a working group meets an objection where everyone understands the issue and acknowledges it is a real shortcoming of the proposed solution, but the majority believes that accommodating it is not worth the trade-off of fixing the problem. An objector may say that protocol X is much more complicated than protocol Y, that Y is elegant and easy to code, and that X is a hack. The group may answer that a great deal of code similar to X already exists and that the risk to interoperability with an untested solution is not worth the advantages of the well-understood protocol X. If the chair finds, in their technical judgement, that the issue has truly been considered and that the group has concluded the trade-off is worth making even in the face of continued objection, the chair can declare rough consensus.

The RFC notes that this portrays rough consensus as a fallback, and in one sense it is: a working group behaves as if striving for full consensus and treats rough consensus as exception processing for cases where the objecting person still feels strongly that their objection is valid. But in the IETF it is more often the norm that someone is unsatisfied with a decision. When a participant says that the solution is not their favourite but they can live with it, that participant is not in the rough part; the group reached consensus. It is rough only when the chair has to declare that an unsatisfied person still has an open issue but the group has answered the objection.

A conclusion of only rough consensus relies heavily on the judgement of the person calling it. The group must truly consider and weigh an issue before an objection can be dismissed. The chair has to decide that the group took the objection seriously, examined the ramifications of not making a change, and that the outcome does not fail the technical requirements of the work. To do that the chair needs a good idea of the purpose and architecture of the work, perhaps from the charter or a published requirements document, and may consult other experts. The chair can get it wrong, and the conclusion is always appealable, but the chair must use their judgement. What cannot happen is basing the decision solely on hearing a large number of voices saying the objection is not valid, because that is simply taking a vote. A valid justification has to be made.

The RFC says this is a change from how rough consensus has sometimes been characterised. RFC 1603 described it as the dominant view of the group, allowed consensus to be determined by balloting, humming or any other means, and said that dominance is not to be determined on the basis of volume or persistence but a more general sense of agreement. RFC 2418 added that 51% of the working group does not qualify as rough consensus and that 99% is better than rough. This document disagrees that counting heads can determine consensus. Counting might give a good guess, but it can allow important minority views to get lost in the noise, and one of the strengths of a consensus model is that minority views are addressed.

Any finding of rough consensus has to give a reasoned explanation to the people raising the issue of why their concern is not going to be accommodated. A good outcome is that the objector understands the decision and accepts it. If the objector feels the issue is essential they always have the option of filing an appeal, and a technical error is always a valid basis for one. Simply having a large majority agree to dismiss an objection is not enough: the group must have honestly considered it and evaluated that other issues weighed sufficiently against it.
sections.plainLanguage: A group can accept that a problem is real and still decide that fixing it costs more than it is worth. The chair then has to explain why, in technical terms, and that explanation is what counts, not the number of people who agree.

sections.title: Humming Starts the Conversation
sections.content:
The IETF does not vote, and in some ways it cannot, because it is not a membership organisation and it is nearly impossible to work out who would get a vote for any given question. It has no members, only participants, and it often recruits additional implementers and experts into working groups so that broader views are represented. Final decisions are supposed to be taken on the mailing list, which reinforces the idea that consensus comes from looking at open issues rather than counting heads. Informal polls are taken occasionally to get a sense of the direction of the discussion, but they are not treated as votes that decide the issue.

The RFC says that more and more people treat a hum as an anonymous vote, with some chairs calling for a hum on every question and judging the result by the loudest hum, saying that lots of hums for one choice and few for another means there is rough consensus for the first. That misses the important points and is almost certainly mis-assessing the consensus.

There are good reasons to hum. One is pragmatic: a chair facing a room that seems diametrically opposed can take a hum to find a starting point, to see whether one choice already has a stronger base of support. Sometimes it shows that the room is not as contentious as it looked, that a few voices had been especially loud. If the hum shows that one choice has significant support, it may be easier to start by asking the people who think that choice is bad to say why it is problematic, and the group can then see whether any of those objections are showstoppers. All the hum does is give the chair a starting point.

Another good reason is that it lets the chair take the temperature of the room. A smaller bunch of loud hums for one choice and a larger number of non-committal hums for another might mean that some people believe there are serious problems with the more popular choice, so starting with the less popular one may get to consensus faster. This can be misleading or even abused, because some people hum louder than others and a quiet hum may turn out to be a showstopper. But taking the hum is about how to start the conversation, and the hum begins the discussion rather than ending it.

A show of hands could do all of this, and on a mailing list a different kind of polling would be needed. The symbolic reason for humming is that a show of hands may leave the impression that the number of people matters in some formal way, and with less experienced participants that can reinforce the mistaken notion that a vote is taking place. The advantage of a hum is that it makes it clear the chair is simply working out the direction of the conversation.

Any informal polling has a misuse. If the chair is already convinced the group has consensus, there is little reason to poll, and polling can discourage those in the minority from voicing concerns in the face of a majority that wants to move forward. The right move is often to say that it sounds as if there is consensus for choice A and ask whether anyone has concerns. A chair may also want to check that there is a real base of support for new work, but this has pitfalls too: someone may be dissuaded from raising an essential concern, or some may hum along with the crowd without being committed. The formulation and even the order of the questions can have huge effects on the outcome, so any poll should be used to prompt discussion and questions rather than to conclude the matter.

Sometimes the result is an even split, which in practice means it does not matter where the chair starts, and working groups have used a coin flip to decide which proposal to start with. That does not mean the coin flip determined the outcome: if a fatal technical flaw is found in the solution that won the flip, the group still has to address the issue raised or abandon that solution and find another. Rough consensus on the technical points is always required, and any way to find a place to start gets to the beginning of the discussion, not the end.
sections.plainLanguage: A hum shows the chair which way to start talking. It is not a vote, and the wording and order of the questions change the result, so it should be used to get people talking rather than to close a question.

sections.title: Two Extremes That Show the Rule
sections.content:
The first extreme is a large working group with over 100 active participants and broad agreement to go forward with a protocol. A few participants say the protocol will cause congestion and has no mechanism to back off, and object to going forward without one. The objection is met with silence on the mailing list. There is no consensus. Even if the chair makes a last call and 100 people reply that the document is ready, if the open issue has not been addressed there is still no consensus, not even rough consensus. It is the existence of the unaddressed open issue, not the number of people, that is determinative. You can have rough consensus with issues that have been purposely dismissed, but not with ones that have been ignored.

This brings back the careful use of a poll at the end of a discussion. If a diligent chair has heard person X raise an objection and heard answers from many others that really address it, and the objection keeps coming up, the chair might take a hum. If only a single objecting hum is heard, even a loud one, against everyone humming that the objection has been answered, the chair has good reason to believe it was addressed. But to say immediately afterwards that it sounds as if there is rough consensus is at best slipshod. What the chair needs to say is that the only objection heard is the one from person X, that the group has answered it fully, and that unless a different objection comes forward there is rough consensus to move on. That makes clear the consensus came from the discussion, not from the hum. And even if no particular person is still standing up for an issue, that does not mean an issue can be ignored: if someone who is not an active participant raises a substantive issue and then disappears, the issue still has to be addressed.

The second extreme is the reverse, and the RFC calls it the real mind-bender. Consider a very small working group with half a dozen truly active participants who are experts, and everybody else following along without contributing. The active members agree on a protocol document that is likely to be widely adopted. One active member objects to a section: the protocol uses a well-known algorithm, but the objector has an elegant alternative that works especially well on their hardware. The others say that the current one is well understood, widely implemented and works perfectly acceptably, and that there is always risk in a new algorithm. The chair judges that the issue has been addressed and declares rough consensus to keep the current solution.

Then the objector, unhappy that their preferred solution was not chosen, recruits one hundred people, mostly colleagues who never participated, and gets them all to post that the elegant algorithm in section Z should be used instead. The chair queries each of them, asking whether they have further information that indicates something different, and gets silence: they thought they were voting and have no answer to give. The chair can then say that the objections have been sufficiently answered, the objectors seem uninterested in participating, and that, albeit rough in the extreme, there is rough consensus to go with the current solution.

The same principle holds however new or credible the objectors seem. The chair is trying to discover whether objections have been addressed or whether there are still open issues. If the new voices are developers directly involved in the technology rather than colleagues from a sales department, the principle is the same: if the objection has been addressed and the new voices are not giving informed responses to it, they can justifiably be called in the rough. Only sufficiently well-informed responses that justify the position taken really count. The RFC calls this the degenerate case and a clear sign of something pathological, but it is exactly what rough consensus is suited to guard against, namely vote stuffing. The correct outcome is to look at the very weak signal against the huge background noise in order to find the rough consensus, even though it is the hardest call for a chair to make and would be very difficult for an appeals body to sort out.
sections.plainLanguage: An objection that nobody answers stops the document, however many people say yes. And a hundred people saying yes cannot undo an objection that was properly answered, however many people say no.

sections.title: Conclusion
sections.content:
The RFC says that although it talks a good deal about what chairs, working groups and other participants might do to achieve rough consensus, it is not really about process and procedures. It describes a way of thinking about how decisions are made. A show of hands can be useful, and it can also be quite damaging and result in terrible decisions. A device like a hum can avoid those pitfalls, and it can also be a poorly disguised vote. The point is to get people thinking about how decisions are reached so that the dangers of majority rule are avoided and rough consensus decisions with the best technical outcomes are reached.

Its Security Considerations section contains a single quotation from Lao Tzu: he who defends with love will be secure.
sections.plainLanguage: The aim is to reach the best technical answer, not to reach an answer by counting. The RFC is a reminder about how to think, not a rulebook.

viz.caption: WHAT A HUM IS FOR, AND WHAT IT IS NOT

items.title: Finding a starting point
items.text: The hum shows which option has more support, so the discussion can begin with the objections to it.

items.title: Taking the temperature
items.text: A few loud hums for one option can mean that some people think the popular option has real problems.

items.title: Not a vote
items.text: Judging the loudest hum misreads what a hum is for, and mis-assesses the consensus.

items.title: The pitfalls
items.text: Some people hum louder than others, and the wording and order of the questions change the result.

items.title: A poll can silence a minority
items.text: A poll taken when the chair already senses consensus may stop the minority from raising concerns.

cells: An unaddressed objection met with silence leaves no consensus, not even rough consensus.
The open issue decides, not the head count.
The new voices give no informed response, so the objection still counts as answered.
Vote stuffing cannot change the outcome.
